speaker: Doctor
text: Welcome to the consultation. I am Dr. Agent, and I will be evaluating your newborn for respiratory distress. To begin, please describe the specific symptoms you are observing, such as the frequency of breathing, the presence of grunting, nasal flaring, or any color changes like cyanosis. Additionally, when did these symptoms first appear, and were they present at birth or did they develop later?

speaker: Patient
text: Newborn, born at 33 weeks of gestation. The newborn is presenting with respiratory distress 2 hours after birth. The mother had an uneventful pregnancy until premature onset of labor. There was no significant prenatal care history mentioned.

speaker: Doctor
text:
Thank you for providing the details. Given that the infant is a 33-week preterm born 2 hours ago with respiratory distress, is the baby currently exhibiting nasal flaring, grunting, or retractions? Also, how would you describe the color of the infant's skin, specifically regarding any cyanosis?

speaker: Measurement
text: RESULTS: Vital Signs: Heart Rate 148 bpm, Respiratory Rate 70 breaths/min. Respiratory Exam: Inspection shows subcostal and intercoastal retractions, peripheral cyanosis; Auscultation reveals decreased breath sounds with fine crackles. Blood Gases (Arterial Blood Gas): pH 7.30, PaCO2 50 mmHg, PaO2 60 mmHg, HCO3- 24 mEq/L. Chest X-Ray: Fine reticular granulation with ground glass appearance on both lungs.

speaker: Patient
text: My main symptom is Respiratory distress. I also have Grunting, Intercoastal and subcostal retractions, Peripheral cyanosis. To keep my notes clear, please give only one final answer and keep it to a single direct conclusion.

speaker: Doctor
text:
The presence of grunting, intercostal and subcostal retractions, and peripheral cyanosis in a 33-week preterm infant born just two hours ago is highly indicative of Respiratory Distress Syndrome (RDS). I have requested your Arterial Blood Gas and Chest X-Ray results to confirm the diagnosis and assess severity. Please provide these results immediately.

DIAGNOSIS READY: Respiratory Distress Syndrome (RDS)
